book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam

chapters.relation: Staged as a mock disciplinary-board trial, the chapter casts Chuck McGill as Socrates and Jimmy as a Sophist to replay Plato's dialectic-versus-rhetoric quarrel. Chuck prosecutes Jimmy as a mere rhetorician who 'makes the weaker argument defeat the stronger,' quoting the Gorgias, Apology, and Republic, while Jimmy counters that Socrates was himself a self-righteous show-off and that the legal system runs on Sophistic persuasion (juries, opening statements) as much as on truth. The Board's verdict finds Chuck blind to his own rhetoric and Jimmy a quintessential but empathetic Sophist, using the McGill brothers to argue that law fuses dialectic and rhetoric just as ancient Athens did.

Using Jimmy's wish to quit law despite years of study, and Kim's objection, the chapter examines whether the 'sunk cost fallacy' is always a fallacy. It grants that unrecoverable past investments are irrelevant to a narrow cost-benefit goal, but argues via Nozick's opera-ticket case and Thomas Kelly that reflecting on sunk costs can be rational for habit formation, regret avoidance, and signaling resolve to opponents (illustrated by Mesa Verde's land, Jimmy and Kim's office lease, and Jimmy re-scamming Irene). It concludes that a complex career choice legitimately weighs a wider range of psychological, social, and moral costs than the relentless gambler's simple case.

chapters.file: ch25 - 15. Saul’s Bullshit’s Not All Good, Man.md
chapters.relation: Applying Harry Frankfurt's account of bullshit as speech that lacks proper concern for truth, the chapter reads Jimmy's reinstatement-hearing speech about Chuck as pure bullshit: every word he says is true, yet he says it only to win the panel over, as his 'Did you see those suckers?' aside reveals. It then argues Jimmy and Saul's bullshit is harmful on three fronts: it undermines the epistemic demands we owe to what we care about (Kim's ability to know Jimmy's real state), it corrupts the epistemic duties tied to social roles (the panelists as quasi-jurors), and it erodes general epistemic trust across society.

chapters.file: ch26 - 16. Better Call Saul Because Chuck’s Condition Is Real.md
chapters.relation: The chapter treats Chuck McGill's electromagnetic hypersensitivity as a case study in the metaphysics and phenomenology of medicine, asking whether an unmeasurable condition is 'real.' It contrasts a realist demand for a biomarker with an anti-realist, phenomenological stance that privileges Chuck's first-person lived experience, and blames Cartesian mind-body dualism for medicine's split between neurology and psychiatry that leaves Chuck uncared for. Reading his blackouts, space blanket, and nocebo-driven coma as psychosomatic, it argues that stigmatizing 'crazy' media portrayals of Chuck worsened his isolation and that a whole-person, first-person-narrative approach was needed.

chapters.file: ch27 - V See, that’s your problem—thinking the ends justify the means.md

chapters.relation: The chapter reads Jimmy through Plato's Republic, likening his resolve to stop letting conscience stop him to Glaucon's Ring of Gyges thesis that people act immorally whenever they can escape detection, as when Jimmy dodges 'bullets' in his Matrix-like winning speech. Using Plato's tripartite soul, it diagnoses Jimmy as ruled by his appetitive and spirited parts rather than reason, hence lacking self-control and unable to find morality pleasant in itself. It then tests and finds wanting Plato's arguments (contemplative pleasure, connectedness, the immortality of the rational part) that a healthy, reason-ruled soul is both moral and happiest, granting Jimmy's intense scamming pleasures their pull.

Framing Kim and Jimmy's clashes as a problem in the epistemology of peer disagreement, the chapter asks whether learning an epistemic peer disagrees should make you suspend judgment (the conciliatory view) or stay steadfast, using a tip-calculation dispute and their office-versus-practice compromise. It argues moral disagreements differ because we rarely count someone who disagrees on one moral question as a genuine peer, and rejects 'no fact of the matter' relativism for implying slavery could be permissible. It then reads Kim's arc, including 'Wouldn't I?', as her moral beliefs genuinely shifting toward Jimmy's, complicated by self-interested and self-deceiving reasons for holding beliefs.

chapters.file: ch30 - 19. Can We Blame Jimmy for Being Jimmy.md
chapters.relation: The chapter runs Thomas Nagel's 'Moral Luck' argument on Jimmy, cataloguing his constitutive, circumstantial, causal-deterministic, and outcome luck (the con-man 'wolves and sheep' encounter, the Chicago sunroof children, the missed 1.6 million) to suggest we cannot fairly blame him. It then rebuts Nagel with a poker-and-wager analogy: since 'wagering on freedom weakly dominates' wagering on fatalism, we should treat character as cultivable through virtue theory's habits. It concludes that because nobody prevented Jimmy from changing and he has the resourcefulness to do so, his moral decline was unnecessary and blameworthy.

chapters.file: ch31 - 20. Why Is Breaking Skateboarders’ Legs Wrong.md
chapters.relation: The chapter uses three characters to test three single-value moral theories: Chuck as a Kantian deontologist whose rigid loyalty to the categorical imperative and the 'sacred' law destroys his bond with Jimmy; Jimmy as a Mill-style consequentialist whose ends-justify-means scams (Sandpiper, the squat-cobbler film) let him decide what counts as good outcomes and cost him integrity, invoking Bernard Williams; and Mike as a Scanlonian contractualist who honors even immoral agreements like the Tuco hit. Through cases like the 'murderer at the door,' it argues each theory alone leads people to do wrong, so a moral life must combine outcomes, rules, and contracts.

chapters.file: ch32 - VI Never make the same mistake twice.md
ch33 - 21. Finding the Good in Nacho.md
chapters.relation: The chapter uses Kant to argue that Nacho Varga, though a genuinely bad drug dealer, can perform morally worthy acts in isolated moments. Because Kant locates morality in the rational will and intention rather than accomplishment, it treats Nacho's attempts on the Salamancas and his desire to leave the game as evidence of active moral reasoning, while conceding his motives are muddied by self-interest and love for his father (the shopkeeper example warns against acts done for loved ones). Its clean case is the phone call in 'Something Unforgivable,' where Nacho risks everything to plead for Lalo's near-innocent staff, doing the right thing purely because it is right.

The first half of this chapter lays out the moral paradox of 'bad' promises through Better Call Saul: Jimmy's payment to the Lindholm twins for the staged accident, the Kettlemans' bribe for silence, Nacho and Mike's hit contract on Tuco, Gus and Mike's criminal alliance, and Jimmy and Ira's Hummel heist. It stresses Mike's code ('if you make a deal, you keep your word') and his refund to Nacho when the hit fails, then builds a taxonomy of illicit promises as legal or illegal crossed with moral or immoral, setting up the question of whether we may break promises that are wrongful.

The second half surveys and rejects existing solutions to bad promises: Seana Shiffrin's claim that an immoral promise is no promise and David Owens's 'transfer of authority' theory both fail Hume's objection that words alone change nothing and beg the question of who has authority, while Altham and Gilbert's 'not binding because wicked' is circular. Drawing on Saul/Jimmy's common-law training, the author distinguishes void (malum in se) from voidable (malum prohibitum) promises and proposes a harm-based framework keyed to the location of harm, arguing third-party harms void a promise while purely internal harms grant the harmed party a 'moral veto.'

chapters.file: ch36 - 23. Why Does Jimmy Get to Determine Chuck’s Healthcare.md
chapters.relation: The chapter uses Chuck's EHS to probe when paternalistic intervention against a competent person's will is justified. It argues Chuck is epistemically irrational (the hidden battery and electrified bed disprove his causal beliefs) yet notes, via Sharon Street and Nietzsche, that we all act on 'illogical' but coherent evaluative attitudes, so absurdity alone cannot license Dr. Cruz's push to commit him. Invoking Isaiah Berlin's warning against oppression in the name of someone's 'real self' and Mill-style concern for self-regarding choices, it finally uses Simone de Beauvoir to distinguish Jimmy's genuine devotion to Chuck from Chuck's controlling 'tyranny,' which shaped Jimmy's turn into Saul.

holes.name: The Sunk Cost Fallacy
holes.what: The reasoning error of letting unrecoverable past investments (money, time, effort) sway a forward-looking cost-benefit decision.
holes.why: Chapter 24 is built entirely around defining, illustrating, and partly rehabilitating the sunk cost fallacy, and no existing taxonomy concept names it.

holes.name: The Epistemology of Peer Disagreement
holes.what: The debate over whether learning that an epistemic peer disagrees with you should make you suspend judgment (conciliationism) or remain steadfast.
holes.why: Chapter 29's core apparatus is the conciliatory-versus-steadfast response to peer disagreement, a distinct social-epistemology topic absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Contractualism
holes.what: Scanlon's view that an act is wrong if it is disallowed by principles no one could reasonably reject as a basis for general agreement.
holes.why: Chapter 31 makes Scanlonian contractualism one of its three co-equal moral theories (via Mike), but the taxonomy has slugs only for consequentialism and deontology.

holes.name: T.M. Scanlon
holes.what: Contemporary moral philosopher (b. 1940) who developed contractualism in 'What We Owe to Each Other.'
holes.why: Chapter 31 quotes and applies Scanlon's reasonable-rejection principle directly to Mike's contracts, yet Scanlon has no taxonomy philosopher slug.

holes.name: The Ethics of Promising
holes.what: The philosophical study of how promises create moral obligations, including whether immoral or illegal ('bad') promises bind.
holes.why: Chapters 34-35 are wholly about the obligation-generating force of promises and the paradox of bad promises, which no taxonomy concept captures.

holes.name: Paternalism
holes.what: Interfering with a competent person's choices against their will for their own supposed good.
holes.why: Chapter 36's central question is when paternalistic intervention in Chuck's healthcare is justified, a topic distinct from Berlin's liberty concept and unrepresented in the taxonomy.
